articles.title: Node.js Chatbot API Endpoint Selection for Media Moderation (and Why Schemas Win)
articles.excerpt: Node.js Chatbot API Endpoint Selection for Media Moderation (and Why Schemas Win) Short answer: For a Node.js media-moderation chatbot, choose a synchronous API endpoint that returns schema-validated…
articles.body: Node.js Chatbot API Endpoint Selection for Media Moderation (and Why Schemas Win) Short answer: For a Node.js media-moderation chatbot, choose a synchronous API endpoint that returns schema-validated classifications, then put idempotency, retries, and human review in your own service boundary. A moderation chatbot is the wrong mental model for this job. The application receives a report about media, classifies it before a human review, and must preserve an auditable decision trail. That constraint makes the best endpoint the one that can return a validated, schema-shaped decision synchronously, with a retry strategy that cannot create a second review record. The endpoint name is secondary.

articles.title: The agent left the debug print in the shipped handler, and the green suite could not see it
articles.excerpt: The agent traced an auth mismatch by dropping a console.log("token=", token) into the request handler. It found the real cause — the interceptor attached a stale credential after refresh — patched it,…
articles.body: The agent traced an auth mismatch by dropping a console.log("token=", token) into the request handler. It found the real cause — the interceptor attached a stale credential after refresh — patched it, ran the suite, reported green, and we merged. The debug print stayed behind. Nobody flagged it because the tests had nothing to check. A logging call changes no return value, throws nothing, and asserts against nothing, so a green suite proves the control path ran; it says nothing about whether scratch diagnostics were removed along the way. A print has no assertion target Most unit tests pin behavior: the function returns X, the queue receives Y, the error path throws Z. A diagnostic line sits outside all of those.

articles.title: Dockerize a Go Microservice in Under an Hour
articles.excerpt: I compiled 20 Go microservices with their CI pipelines and found that 16 of them failed to start inside a container because they shipped the source tree instead of a compiled binary. The fix is the sa…
articles.body: I compiled 20 Go microservices with their CI pipelines and found that 16 of them failed to start inside a container because they shipped the source tree instead of a compiled binary. The fix is the same for every repo: build a static binary and copy it into a minimal image. ## 1. Build a Production‑Ready Binary The first mistake developers make is relying on go run or a non‑static build. Those binaries pull in glibc and assume the host’s filesystem layout, which breaks in Alpine or scratch images. # Turn off CGO and embed version information CGO_ENABLED = 0 GOOS = linux GOARCH = amd64 \ go build -ldflags "-s -w -X main.version= $( git rev-parse --short HEAD ) " \ -o ./bin/app ./cmd/server markdown CGO_ENABLED=0 forces a fully static binary.

articles.title: I banned arithmetic in my invoicing app and enforced it with an AST test
articles.excerpt: The quoting and invoicing app I built has a rule that looks odd at first: the app package is not allowed to do arithmetic. No +, no -, no *, no /, no float, and no Decimal(...) outside a short list of…
articles.body: The quoting and invoicing app I built has a rule that looks odd at first: the app package is not allowed to do arithmetic. No + , no - , no * , no / , no float , and no Decimal(...) outside a short list of named files. Every money figure comes from a separate engine, quote_to_cash : one function prices a set of lines ( compute_totals ), a few more work out what's paid and outstanding. The app above it, a Next.js front end over a thin FastAPI layer with a SQLite file per tenant, can store figures, show them and send them on. It can't make new ones. The reason is practical. A quote total that the API worked out one way and the PDF another is a bug a customer finds before I do. If only one module can produce a figure, the two can't disagree.

articles.title: Pick which ResizeObserverEntry field your test should read
articles.excerpt: If a ResizeObserver-based test fails, the problem is often not the browser but the measurement you asked for. ResizeObserverEntry exposes different boxes and units: contentBoxSize (content area), bord…
articles.body: If a ResizeObserver-based test fails, the problem is often not the browser but the measurement you asked for. ResizeObserverEntry exposes different boxes and units: contentBoxSize (content area), borderBoxSize (outer element footprint), and devicePixelContentBoxSize (content in device pixels). Each field answers a different diagnostic question. Implementation decision Start your test by naming the edge you intend to verify. The decision helper in the article is a tiny deterministic policy: it picks contentBoxSize when the question is about the available content area, borderBoxSize when the outer layout footprint matters, and devicePixelContentBoxSize when physical pixels matter.

articles.title: Why your App Store Connect and Google Play Console numbers never match (and never match your analytics)
articles.excerpt: I build a few apps on the side, and every morning I opened App Store Connect, Play Console and my analytics, and no two of them agreed. The store counts a download when the app gets installed. Your an…
articles.body: I build a few apps on the side, and every morning I opened App Store Connect, Play Console and my analytics, and no two of them agreed. While building my own dashboard I had to find out why, one number at a time. These are the reasons I found. The store counts downloads, your analytics counts opens The store counts a download when the app gets installed. Your analytics only sees someone after they open the app with your SDK running. Everyone who downloads and never opens it is in the store number and nowhere else. So your analytics "new users" will be lower than store downloads, and that's normal. "Downloads" means different things on each store On the App Store, first-time downloads and redownloads are separate numbers.

articles.title: PDF/UA on 1,212 public-sector PDFs from 12 countries: what an automatic fix solves (15 %) and what it can't
articles.excerpt: Run a PDF through veraPDF with the PDF/UA-1 profile and you get a list of failed rules. Some of them are a two-line change in the document catalog. Others mean the file has no tags at all and has to b…
articles.body: Run a PDF through veraPDF with the PDF/UA-1 profile and you get a list of failed rules. Some of them are a two-line change in the document catalog. Others mean the file has no tags at all and has to be exported again from its source. The report does not tell you which is which. We measured it on real documents: 1,212 PDFs published by public bodies in 12 countries (Canada, the US, Finland, France, Spain, Norway, the UK, Australia, Ireland, Sweden, Belgium and Portugal) — councils, agencies, universities and ministries that are under some web accessibility obligation. This is not legal advice and says nothing about any organisation's compliance; it only shows which PDF/UA failures are cheap to fix and which are not.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.body: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's a still image, video, audio, or text - that "has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence" to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants' ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad … Read the full story at The Verge.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

articles.title: Medusa's eye, Halloween fireballs and more: 5 skywatching targets to look out for this spooky season
articles.excerpt: Five spooky skywatching targets perfect for naked eye stargazing this Halloween!
articles.body: The spooky season is officially here! To celebrate, we've put together a list of five Halloween-themed skywatching targets that you can enjoy with nothing but the naked eye or binoculars and, of course, clear skies. Over millennia, the night sky has helped shape human beliefs. In return, we have imprinted our myths, stories and perceptions upon it, seeing monsters and mythology in the twinkling lights of the stars and assigning sinister aspects to innocent cosmic objects. Many of these ghostly impressions and meanings have survived to the present day. Here are a few of our favorites. The Pleiades open star cluster Don't be fooled by their beauty; the blue-white stars of the Pleiades are dripping in spooky lore.
